abstract: Summary Photosynthetic protein complexes in thylakoid membranes disassemble during leaf senescence, leading to a decline in photosynthetic efficiency. However, the mechanisms by which these protein complexes in chloroplast thylakoid membranes modulate leaf senescence are poorly understood. This study investigated the roles of Arabidopsis thaliana STN7 and STN8 kinases during leaf senescence using proteomic tools, characterizing STN7 and STN8 overexpressors and loss-of-function mutants. During leaf senescence, proteins involved in photosynthesis-associated processes decreased, while those related to lipid metabolism and jasmonic acid–mediated stress responses increased. The abundance and phosphorylation of the thylakoid membrane proteome were regulated by STN7, but not by STN8. Thirty-four STN7 target proteins overlapped with senescence-associated proteins in the wild type, most of which are related to the photosynthetic protein apparatus. Three out of nine mutants defective in STN7 downstream targets ( lfnr2 , tsp9 , and riq2 ) exhibited accelerated leaf senescence based on chlorophyll a/b ratio measurements and photochemical analyses. Photosynthetic complex formation was normal in all STN7 target protein loss-of-function mutants, indicating the absence of feedback regulation upstream of STN7 during photosynthetic complex assembly. Overall, the data reveal that STN7 is a major kinase component in signaling cascades that link photosynthetic complex formation and leaf senescence.

Cells were lysed initially in Buffer A (10 mM HEPES, pH 8.0, 1.5 mM MgCl

The bound phosphopeptides were eluted from the beads by incubating in 125 μL of 1:1 ACN/2.5% ammonia in 2 mM phosphate buffer (pH 10) for 1.5 min. The eluted phosphopeptides were acidified immediately with 10% TFA and dried.

10 μg of global peptides (Ca. 8%) from each of the 24 fractions and all of the enriched phosphopepide from each of the 12 fractions were injected. All peptide samples were analyzed by Q Exactive Orbitrap mass spectrometer (Thermo Fisher Scientific, Bremen, Germany) at the Center for Proteogenome Research coupled to a modified dual-online nanoACQUITY UPLC system (Waters, Milford, MA).

The dual-online UPLC system was equipped with two capillary analytical columns (75 μm × 100 cm) and two solid phase extraction columns (150 μm × 3 cm) that were prepared by acetonitrile slurry packing frit-ended fused silica capillaries with C18 resin (3 μm, 300 Å, Jupiter, Phenomenex). The two capillary analytical columns were enclosed by a semi-rigid gasline heater (1/4″, 90 cm, WATLOW, USA) for maintaining column temperature at 60°C (Hyung et al., 2011). The electrospray ionization (ESI) emitter was manufactured by chemical etching method using fused silica capillary (15 μm × 4 cm).

The solvent A and solvent B were 0.1% formic acid in water and 0.1% formic acid in ACN, respectively. The column flow rate was 300 nL/min and two different gradients were used: a 180 min linear gradient (1-40 % sol B over 160 min, 40-80 % over 5 min, 80 % for 10 min and holding at 1 % for 5 min) for the 24 fraction global peptide samples and a 240 min linear gradient (1-50 % sol B over 220 min, 50-80 % over 5 min, 80 % for 10 min and holding at 1 % for 5 min) for the 12 fraction phosphopeptide samples.
The eluted peptide from the LC were ionized through a home-built nano-electrospray source at the electric potential of 2.4 kV and the desolvation capillary temperature was set to 250°C. MS precursor ion scans (m/z 400 - 2,000 Th) were acquired at the resolution of 70,000 with an automated gain control (AGC) target value of 1.0 × 10
6
and a maximum ion injection time (IT) of 20 ms. The MS/MS data for up to the 10 most abundant ions with charge ≥2 were acquired in a data dependent mode with an isolation window of ±0.8 Th, the exclusion duration of 30 s, and at a normalized collision energy (NCE) of 35 for higher energy collisional dissociation (HCD). The MS/MS scans were acquired at a resolution of 17,500 for the global peptide analysis and at a resolution of 35,000 for the phosphopeptide analysis with a fixed first m/z of 120 Th. Maximum ion injection times were 60 ms and 120 ms for MS/MS scan of global peptide and phosphopeptide samples, respectively. Automated gain control (AGC) target value was set to 1.0 × 10
6
for both global and phosphopeptide MS/MS scan.
LC-MS/MS data analysis
Liquid chromatography with tandem mass spectrometry (LC-MS/MS) data were first processed by the multiplexed post experimental monoisotopic mass refinement (mPE-MMR) method, as previously described.
64
The refined data were searched against uniprot
Arabidopsis thaliana
reference database (released November 2015; 33,434 entries) and common contaminants (179 entries) using MS-GF + search engine (V9949).
65
Semi-tryptic cleavage allowance and precursor mass tolerance of 10 ppm were used for MS-GF + parameters. For global proteome analysis, TMT to lysine, and N-terminus and carbamidomethylation to cysteine, were used as static modifications. Oxidation to methionine and deamidation to asparagine and glutamine were used as variable modifications. For phosphoproteome analysis, the variable modifications of phosphorylation to serine, threonine, or tyrosine were added. The peptide spectrum matches (PSMs) were obtained using a false discovery rate (FDR) of 0.01. For phosphoproteome data, an additional search for unassigned spectra was performed after excluding PSMs from MS-GF + using MODplus search engine.
66
The variables, parameters, and databases of MODplus were the same as those of MS-GF+. The PSMs at FDR of 0.01 from MODplus were also used for analysis.
Protein and phosphosite inference
The peptides with 100% precursor isolation purity (PIP) detected in more than half of the experiments (≥2) were used for protein inference. The peptides were rolled up to infer the protein groups using bipartite graph analysis.
75
Representative proteins for each group were selected from those with the largest number of peptides. For the analysis of the global proteome, the protein groups peptide numbers ≥2, maximum protein coverage ≥25%, and unique coding-genes within groups were used. For phosphoproteome data, peptides were rolled up to infer the phosphosite groups, instead of protein groups. Thus, the representative phosphosites of protein for each group was selected. The phosphosite groups with peptide numbers ≥1 and unique coding-genes within groups were used for phosphoproteome analysis.

After mapping normalized intensities to PSMs, PSMs with 100% PIP were selected for further analysis, as described above. When multiple PSMs had PIP = 100, the average intensity was calculated for the quantification of the peptide. To remove the batch effects of TMT experiments, selected peptides were normalized following three steps: 1) the intensity matrices of these peptides were log
2
-transformed and normalized by the mean of each peptide in the corresponding TMT experiment; 2) the normalized matrices of each TMT experiment were stacked into a single column of data and then merged into a master matrix by concatenating the columns horizontally; and 3) the master matrix was quantile normalized and transformed into the peptide intensity matrices of each TMT experiment.
Identification of DEPeptides, DEPs, and DEPsites
The peptides having intensity values more than 50% of each comparison condition were used for identifying differentially expressed peptides (DEPeptides). The t-statistical values and log
2
-fold-changes were first obtained using Student’s t-test and median-ratio for each comparison. Empirical null distribution of t-statistical values was then estimated from random permutated intensity matrix (1,000 times). The adjusted
p
-values (Pt) were calculated by two-tailed tests for the observed t-statistical values using the empirical distributions. The peptides with Pt < 0.05 and an absolute value of log2-fold-changes >0.58 (1.5-fold-change) were selected as DEPeptides. The protein groups with DEPeptide numbers ≥2, except proteins having both up- and down-regulated DEPeptides, were identified as differentially expressed proteins (DEPs) in the global proteome. For the phosphoproteome, the phosphosite groups with DEPeptide numbers ≥2, except for phosphosites having both up- and down-regulated DEPeptides, were identified as differentially expressed phosphosites (DEPsites).
Functional enrichment analysis
To identify cellular processes and pathways represented by DEPs- and DEPsites-containing proteins, functional enrichment analysis was performed using the Database for Annotation, Visualization and Integrated Discovery (DAVID) software.

The terms with
p

Introduction
Photosynthesis is a fundamental physiological process that supports the biosynthesis of plant biomass. The carbohydrate products of photosynthesis accumulate in regions of active growth within the plant, as well as in various sink tissues and storage organs, including fruits, seeds, roots, and tubers. Photosynthesis predominantly occurs in the chlorophyll-rich leaves, which house chloroplasts responsible for the plant’s green pigmentation. During leaf senescence, photosynthetic products are redistributed to different sink tissues, such as cereal grains. Consequently, senescence plays a pivotal role in determining agricultural crop yield.
1
,
2
Leaf senescence is a complex process involving the degradation of chlorophyll, the breakdown of macromolecules, and the remobilization of nutrients. It is regulated by a multitude of external stimuli, including day length, temperature, and drought, as well as internal signals like oxidative stress and senescence-associated gene expression.
3
These events result in the alteration of leaf color and the eventual abscission of the leaf. Chlorophyll is a key molecule that captures light energy and transfers it to the photosystem reaction centers, driving the synthesis of energy-rich compounds. Thus, the loss of chlorophyll is closely associated with the reduction of photosynthetic efficiency during leaf senescence.
4
,
5
,
6
Photosynthetic protein complexes are spatially organized and functionally coupled in the thylakoid membranes of chloroplasts. Two major complexes, photosystem I (PSI) and photosystem II (PSII), capture and convert light energy into chemical energy through a series of electron transport reactions mediated by various plant pigments and accessory proteins.
The PSII complex is associated with light-harvesting chlorophyll
b
-binding (LHCB) monomers and light-harvesting complex II (LHCII) trimers, which act as light energy donors. These complexes are predominantly located in the inner regions of the grana stacks of thylakoid membranes. The PSI complex is associated with monomeric LHCA proteins that are mainly found in the peripheral regions of the grana stacks and the stroma lamellae. Light-harvesting complexes (LHCs) comprise chlorophyll-binding proteins, also known as antennae. These proteins absorb light energy and transfer it to the reaction centers of PSII.
7
,
8
,
9
,
10
,
11
Light absorption by chlorophyll in the thylakoid membrane triggers electron transport via PSI and PSII. These protein complexes have reaction centers where electrons are excited and transferred to different carriers. There are two electron transport pathways: linear electron flow (LEF) and cyclic electron flow (CEF). LEF involves both PSII and PSI, producing oxygen, energy, and carbohydrates. In LEF, light excites an electron in PSII, which is transferred to pheophytin, then to the cytochrome
b
6
f
(Cyt
b
6
f
) complex, which pumps protons to make ATP. The electron then reaches PSI, where light re-excites it and passes it to ferredoxin, then to NADP+ reductase, which makes NADPH. ATP and NADPH are used to fix carbon dioxide into carbohydrates in the Calvin cycle. Water splitting by the oxygen-evolving complex replenishes electrons in PSII. CEF involves only PSI and produces only energy. In CEF, light excites an electron in PSI, which is transferred to ferredoxin, then back to the Cyt
b
6
f
complex, which pumps protons to make ATP. The electron returns to PSI completing the cycle. CEF does not produce NADPH or oxygen but balances ATP and NADPH for the Calvin cycle.
12
Upon the onset of leaf senescence, the photochemical reactions within the two photosystems decline.
13
,
14
Chlorophyll
a
degrades faster than chlorophyll
b
during leaf senescence, resulting in lower light energy input into the photosynthetic complexes and reduced photosynthetic efficiency.
6
,
15
As leaf senescence progresses, the photosynthetic protein complexes in thylakoid membranes disassemble. The Cyt
b
6
f
complex and ATP synthase, which are involved in the photosynthetic electron transport chain, are more susceptible to senescence-induced damage than PSI or PSII. The loss of these complexes affects electron transport and energy production, triggering further disassembly of the photosynthetic complexes.
16
,
17
,
18
Phosphorylation regulates the organization of photosynthetic protein complexes. Two serine/threonine kinases, STATE TRANSITION 7 (STN7) and STATE TRANSITION 8 (STN8), are the main kinases that phosphorylate these complexes.
19
,
20
,
21
They have different substrates and roles. STN7 phosphorylates LHCII upon light exposure, causing it to move from PSII to PSI during state transitions. STN7 is tightly bound to the Cyt
b
6
f
complex in the thylakoid membrane.
22
STN8 phosphorylates D1, D2, CP43, and PsbH, which are core proteins of PSII. STN8-mediated phosphorylation of D1 facilitates its degradation and replacement in PSII repair. STN8 also participates in protein migration in the thylakoid membrane.
23
Although both kinases are involved in organizing photosynthetic protein complexes, they have different roles in leaf senescence, as shown by the different senescence phenotypes of their loss-of-function mutants (
stn7
and
stn8
).
24
While
stn7
mutants display an alteration of photosynthetic protein complex organization, a reduction in CP29 phosphorylation, and an acceleration of leaf senescence, the phenotypes of
stn8
mutants are similar to those of wild-type plants.
24
The mechanisms by which STN7 modulates leaf senescence through biochemical and molecular processes within the thylakoid membrane are still unknown.
This study used proteomic analysis of thylakoid membranes from wild type and
stn7
plants to identify downstream targets of STN7 in leaf senescence, aiming to understand how STN7 controls this process. The study showed that LFNR2, TSP9, and RIQ2 are major downstream targets of STN7 in leaf senescence. These targets did not affect the organization of photosynthetic protein complexes. The data suggest that STN7 signals in one direction and regulates multiple components of the photosynthetic protein complexes during leaf senescence.

STN7 is a primary kinase that regulates leaf senescence
Whole plant phenotypes of wild-type (WT),
stn7
, and
stn8

oeSTN7

oeSTN8

stn7

Figure S1

Figure S1
B). Chlorophyll a/b ratios in
stn7

oeSTN7
had similar ratios to the WT (
Figure 1
A). Chlorophyll
a
is essential for photosynthesis because it donates electrons in the electron transport chain. The lower chlorophyll
a
content in
stn7
suggests that STN7 is important for maintaining chlorophyll
a
levels during leaf senescence. To assess the impact of reduced chlorophyll
a
content in
stn7
on photosynthetic efficiency, we measured the maximum quantum efficiency of PSII (Fv’/Fm’) following dark adaptation of leaves at both DAE18 and DAE30. The findings indicated that, at DAE30, only
stn7
displayed a significantly lower Fv’/Fm’ value compared to the wild type, whereas no significant decrease in Fv’/Fm’ was observed in stn7 at DAE18, and
oeSTN7

Figure 1

and

stn7
mutant compared to the WT. In contrast, this alteration was reversed in
oeSTN7

This suggests that STN7 mainly regulates the accumulation of reactive oxygen species, chlorophyll a/b ratio, and photochemical efficiency during leaf senescence. We further investigated and found that STN7 is responsible for the phosphorylation of LHCII and LHCII-PSI-LHCI complex formation throughout leaf senescence (

As observed in leaf yellowing and photosynthetic efficiency, both the phosphorylation of LHCII and the formation of the LHCII-PSI-LHCI complex were altered in the

oeSTN7

stn7

Proteomic analysis identifies senescence-associated and STN7 target proteins in the thylakoid membrane
As previously mentioned, STN7 plays a central role in leaf senescence as a kinase responsible for regulating photosynthetic protein complexes, with the LHCII complex being its primary target. To explore potential additional STN7 targets in leaf senescence, we performed a comprehensive analysis of the whole thylakoid membrane proteome (referred to as the global proteome) and the phosphorylation-enriched proteome from the thylakoid membrane (referred to as the phosphoproteome). Photosynthetic complexes undergo strong changes during leaf senescence
To elucidate leaf age–dependent protein complex shifts in the thylakoid membrane, we conducted a series of analyses to reconstitute protein complexes using thylakoid membrane proteomics in WT. Differentially regulated proteins during natural leaf aging were identified from the global proteome and phosphoproteome of thylakoid membranes. Among these, 114 proteins were upregulated and 170 were downregulated in thylakoid membrane proteins, while 51 showed up-regulation and 59 displayed down-regulation in thylakoid membrane phosphoproteins (
Figure 3
A). Among these proteins, 14 were common to the global proteome and phosphoproteome in the thylakoid membrane during leaf senescence (
Figure 3
B). Seven proteins (Patellin1 (PATL1), Early Response to Dehydration 14 (ERD14), Catalase 3 (CAT3), Pheophorbide A Oxygenase (PAO), Villin 3 (VLN3), Purple Acid Phosphatase 2 (PAP2), and PLD Regulated Protein 1 (PLDRP1)) showed an increase in both abundance and phosphorylation as leaves aged. This coordination may indicate a regulatory mechanism linked to the aging process. Conversely, six proteins (Reduced Chloroplast Coverage 1 (REC1), Leaf-Type Ferredoxin-NADP+ Oxidoreductase (LFNR2), Pale Yellow Green 7 (PYG7), Thylakoid-soluble Phosphoprotein 9 (TSP9), Copper Response Defect 1 (CRD1), and Light-harvesting-like protein 3.1 (LIL3.1) exhibited a decrease in both abundance and phosphorylation in senescing leaves. This simultaneous upregulation or downregulation suggests coordination between protein levels and phosphorylation status in the thylakoid membrane during leaf aging. Notably, the protein abundance of Photosystem II Subunit P-1 (PSPB1) in the thylakoid membrane showed an increase in abundance but a decrease in phosphorylation during leaf senescence. This differential regulation of PSPB1 implies that the abundance and phosphorylation of PSPB1 are independently regulated or influenced by distinct factors during the leaf aging process.
To understand the biological functions of the proteins that change their abundance and phosphorylation levels in the thylakoid membrane during leaf senescence, we categorized them according to the biological processes they are involved in (
Figure 3
C). Proteins downregulated in both abundance and phosphorylation were enriched in photosynthesis-associated processes, including photosystem I, photosystem II, and chlorophyll metabolic processes. Those with decreased abundance were enriched in processes such as the electron transport chain, H+ transporting ATP synthase complex, and translation. Conversely, proteins increased in the thylakoid membrane showed enrichment in carotenoid biosynthesis, lipid metabolic processes, and jasmonic acid metabolic processes (
Figure 3
C). Based on these observations, we reconstructed the primary biological processes occurring in the thylakoid membrane during leaf senescence (
Figure S6
). Remarkably, proteins within the thylakoid membranes exhibited cohesive behavior, reflecting shared trends indicative of their involvement in the same pathway. For instance, a considerable proportion of proteins related to Cyt
b
6
f
, ATP synthase, the translation machinery, and chlorophyll metabolic processes were downregulated, in contrast to the up-regulation of those involved in plastoglobuli formation and carotenoid metabolism. While protein components of PSI and PSII complexes showed minor changes in abundance during leaf senescence, the phosphorylation of PSII core proteins decreased (
Figure S6
). This decrease in phosphorylation suggests a role for this process in senescence-associated functions of PSII. The simultaneous decrease in abundance of the Cyt
b
6
f
and ATP synthase complexes, along with reduced phosphorylation of PSII, indicates a coordinated decay of photosynthetic protein complexes during leaf senescence. These findings highlight a significant functional and co-regulatory relationship between SAP and SPP during leaf senescence.

Discussion
STN7 is a major kinase that modulates leaf senescence
Phosphorylation is a major post-translational modification of photosynthetic proteins. Phosphorylation of protein components of the photosynthetic apparatus is accomplished by STN7 and STN8. Both these kinases are critical for temporarily reorganizing photosynthetic protein complexes to increase photochemical efficiency under fluctuating light conditions. In addition to light, other plant developmental events influence photochemical efficiency. One such event is leaf senescence, which occurs throughout the lifespan of a plant.

Diverse protein complexes in the thylakoid membrane cooperate in modulating leaf senescence
In the thylakoid membrane, diverse protein complexes participate in maximizing a plant’s fitness when environmental conditions fluctuate. Protein components of various complexes and processes in the thylakoid membrane were identified in senescing leaves. The study identified multiple proteins that were not observed in a previous publication, possibly because our focus was on leaf aging and advances in protein detection techniques. The identified proteins were part of photosynthetic protein complexes and translational machineries, and also involved in plastid organization, pigment synthesis, lipid metabolism, and jasmonic acid–dependent stress-responsive processes. The reconstituted complexes upon leaf aging provided critical clues about how leaf senescence is regulated by molecular events occurring in the thylakoid membrane (
Figure S6
). The majority of proteins in thylakoid membranes are components of photosynthetic protein complexes and plastid-organizing centers. Therefore, the decline of thylakoid-resident proteins was clearly observed during leaf senescence and likely explains the visual changes occurring in senescing leaves. Proteins involved in translation that were adjacent to the thylakoid membrane had increased levels of phosphorylation. Proteins involved in lipid metabolism and stress-responsive protein compartments were upregulated in protein abundance. Multiple biological processes such as a decline in photosynthesis, enforcement of lipid metabolism, and jasmonic acid responses can occur simultaneously in the thylakoid membrane. These findings provide additional insights into how the progression of leaf senescence is modulated by molecular events in the thylakoid membrane, which are distinct from transcription occurring in the nucleus.

STN7 is pivotal for leaf senescence
This study reveals that STN7 is the primary kinase responsible for phosphorylating photosynthetic proteins during leaf senescence, while STN8 plays only a minor role in this process. STN7 modulates the abundance and phosphorylation status of photosynthetic proteins in the thylakoid membrane but does not impact other leaf senescence processes. Our proteomics data (
Table S1
) indicate that the abundance of the STN7 protein itself does not change during leaf senescence; however, its efficacy as a kinase diminishes. STN7 is known to tightly bind to Cyt
b
6
f
in the thylakoid membrane.

As Cyt
b
6
f
begins to degrade during the early stages of leaf senescence, STN7 may dissociate from the Cyt
b
6
f
complex. This dissociation of STN7 from the Cyt
b
6
f
complex can lead to a reduction in the phosphorylation of STN7 targets located near the photosynthetic protein complexes in the thylakoid membrane.
The previous study has revealed that STN7 phosphorylates LFNR and RPS7, in addition to LHCII, in light-illuminated chloroplasts.
57
The phosphorylation by STN7 of its targets exhibited an amino acid preference, with glycine and proline near the phosphorylation sites of LHCII, and glycine and tyrosine were enriched in other STN7 targets. In this study, we also found that STN7 showed a preference for phosphorylating during leaf senescence (
Figure 4
B). Peptides displaying age-associated phosphorylation by STN7 in the thylakoid membrane not only confirmed the presence of glycine at the −2 position from the phosphorylation site, aligning with prior research, but notably, this glycine positioning exhibited a significantly higher prevalence in age-associated phosphorylation by STN7 compared to the broader chloroplast proteomics data. During leaf senescence, it is likely that STN7 exhibits an increased selectivity in phosphorylating proteins within the thylakoid membrane, indicating a more focused and specific phosphorylation pattern during this physiological process.
STN7 acts as a negative regulator of leaf senescence, and therefore keeps the leaf green. However, because STN7 has multiple target proteins, its role in leaf senescence likely extends beyond that of a negative regulator. Sixteen mutants to STN7 target proteins were analyzed in leaf senescence. None of these mutants showed an altered LHCII-PSI-LHCI complex during senescence, which means that STN7 can phosphorylate or regulate their abundance, but the targets of STN7 cannot affect STN7 during leaf senescence. However, LFNR2, TSP9, and RIQ2 did not influence the phosphorylation of LHCII, STN7 protein abundance, or senescence gene expression. In turn, STN7 can act as their kinase, but LFNR2, TSP9, and RIQ2 do not exhibit feedback regulation to STN7 during leaf senescence. Interestingly, we did not observe clear differences in senescence gene expressions in all three mutants, indicating that the regulation of leaf senescence in the thylakoid membrane by STN7 can be distinguished from that in the nucleus. STN7 also regulates the protein abundances of APX4, TL17, LHCA4, and CTPA2, and exploring their roles in leaf senescence could be interesting to unveil novel functions of STN7.
In summary, this study revealed major biological processes in the thylakoid membrane that govern leaf senescence. In the thylakoid membrane, reduced efficiency of photosynthesis-related processes, and increased lipid metabolism and jasmonic acid responses mainly occurred in senescing leaves. STN7 selectively regulated photosynthetic protein complexes during leaf senescence, resulting in delayed leaf aging. This study provides another potential mechanism by which biological processes in the thylakoid membrane specify the progression of leaf senescence, distinct from nuclear gene transcriptional pathways. A major molecular player in the regulation of leaf senescence is the STN7 kinase, which phosphorylates photosynthetic protein complexes during the progression of leaf senescence.

Peptide preparation and TMT labeling
Cells were lysed initially in Buffer A (10 mM HEPES, pH 8.0, 1.5 mM MgCl
2
, 10 mM KCl, 300 mM sucrose, 0.1% NP-40, 0.5 mM PMSF) for 5 min on ice. The lysates were centrifuged at 10,000 × g for 1 min, and the supernatant was collected as cytosolic fraction. Then, the pellets were lysed in Buffer B (20 mM HEPES, pH 8.0, 20% glycerol, 100 mM KCl, 100 mM NaCl, 0.2 mM EDTA, 0.5 mM PMSF). After 10 min on ice, the lysates from the pellets were centrifuged at 10,000 × g for 5 min, and the supernatant was collected as nuclear fraction. After BCA measurement, a total of 200 μg of proteins from each sample were reduced with 10 mM dithiothreitol at 37°C for 45 min, alkylated with 30 mM iodoacetamide in dark at room temperature for 30 min, and diluted with 40 mM ammonium bicarbonate to reach 1 M urea. Then, the sequencing grade trypsin (Promega; Madison; WI) was used to enzymatically digest the proteome at an enzyme to protein ratio of 1 to 20 (w/w) at 37°C overnight. After acidification, the digested peptide mixture was desalted using C18 Macro Spin Columns (HA; 74-4101). Eluted clean peptide samples were dried in a speed vacuum concentrator and kept at − 80°C until TMT labeling. Dried desalted peptides were labeled using 10-plex TMT reagent (Thermo Scientific, Rockford, IL). TMT labeling reaction was performed as per the manufacturer instructions with minor modifications. Briefly, peptide samples were resuspended with 100 mM triethylammonium bicarbonate while TMT reagents were with 40 μL anhydrous acetonitrile. Peptide solution were mixed vigorously with the reagents and kept at room temperature for 2 hours. Finally, TMT-labeled peptides were mixed and then stored at −80° C until peptide fractionation.
Peptide fractionation
The 3 mg pooled 6-plex TMT-labeled peptide sample was fractionated using Agilent 1260 Infinity HPLC system (Agilent, Palo Alto, CA) equipped with a Xbridge C18 analytical column (4.6 mm × 250 mm, 130 Å, 5 μm) and a guard column (4.6 mm × 20 mm, 130 Å, 5μm) as described previously.
72
Mid-pH RPLC fractionation was performed at a flow rate 500 μL/min using solvent A (10 mM TEAB in water, pH 7.5) and solvent B (10 mM TEAB in ACN, pH 7.5). A 115 min gradient was applied as follows: 0% sol B for 10 min, 0-5 % sol B in 10 min, 5-35 % sol B in 60 min, 35-70 % sol B in 15 min, 70 % sol B for 10 min, 70-0 % sol B in 10 min. Every 1 min of the eluent from 15 min to 110 min was divided into 96 fractions, and they were pooled into 24 non-contiguously concatenated fractions. The resultant 24 fractions were dried and stored at −80°C.
Phosphopeptide enrichment
Ca. 92% of 6-plex TMT-labeled peptide fractions were used phosphopeptide enrichment as described previously.

IMAC experiments were performed from 12 fractions obtained by combining two adjacent fractions of 24 fractions (i.e., #1-#2, #3-#4, …, and #23-#24 fraction). Fe
3+

3
solution for 30 min with end-over-end rotation. The resultant Fe
3+
-NTA beads were washed and resuspended in 1:1:1 ACN/MeOH/0.01% acetic acid for aliquoting into 12 microcentrifuge tubes and the beads of each tube was washed with binding buffer (80% ACN/0.1% TFA). Each of the 12 fractions (ca. 230 μg each) was resuspended in 500 μL of binding buffer and then transferred to a tube of the aliquoted beads for phosphopeptide enrichment. 12 fraction samples were reacted for 30 min with end-over-end rotation and then the beads were washed using binding buffer. The bound phosphopeptides were eluted from the beads by incubating in 125 μL of 1:1 ACN/2.5% ammonia in 2 mM phosphate buffer (pH 10) for 1.5 min. The eluted phosphopeptides were acidified immediately with 10% TFA and dried.
LC-MS/MS experiments
10 μg of global peptides (Ca. 8%) from each of the 24 fractions and all of the enriched phosphopepide from each of the 12 fractions were injected. All peptide samples were analyzed by Q Exactive Orbitrap mass spectrometer (Thermo Fisher Scientific, Bremen, Germany) at the Center for Proteogenome Research coupled to a modified dual-online nanoACQUITY UPLC system (Waters, Milford, MA).
73
The dual-online UPLC system was equipped with two capillary analytical columns (75 μm × 100 cm) and two solid phase extraction columns (150 μm × 3 cm) that were prepared by acetonitrile slurry packing frit-ended fused silica capillaries with C18 resin (3 μm, 300 Å, Jupiter, Phenomenex). The two capillary analytical columns were enclosed by a semi-rigid gasline heater (1/4″, 90 cm, WATLOW, USA) for maintaining column temperature at 60°C (Hyung et al., 2011). The electrospray ionization (ESI) emitter was manufactured by chemical etching method using fused silica capillary (15 μm × 4 cm).
74
The solvent A and solvent B were 0.1% formic acid in water and 0.1% formic acid in ACN, respectively. The column flow rate was 300 nL/min and two different gradients were used: a 180 min linear gradient (1-40 % sol B over 160 min, 40-80 % over 5 min, 80 % for 10 min and holding at 1 % for 5 min) for the 24 fraction global peptide samples and a 240 min linear gradient (1-50 % sol B over 220 min, 50-80 % over 5 min, 80 % for 10 min and holding at 1 % for 5 min) for the 12 fraction phosphopeptide samples.
The eluted peptide from the LC were ionized through a home-built nano-electrospray source at the electric potential of 2.4 kV and the desolvation capillary temperature was set to 250°C. MS precursor ion scans (m/z 400 - 2,000 Th) were acquired at the resolution of 70,000 with an automated gain control (AGC) target value of 1.0 × 10
6
and a maximum ion injection time (IT) of 20 ms. The MS/MS data for up to the 10 most abundant ions with charge ≥2 were acquired in a data dependent mode with an isolation window of ±0.8 Th, the exclusion duration of 30 s, and at a normalized collision energy (NCE) of 35 for higher energy collisional dissociation (HCD). The MS/MS scans were acquired at a resolution of 17,500 for the global peptide analysis and at a resolution of 35,000 for the phosphopeptide analysis with a fixed first m/z of 120 Th. Maximum ion injection times were 60 ms and 120 ms for MS/MS scan of global peptide and phosphopeptide samples, respectively. Automated gain control (AGC) target value was set to 1.0 × 10
6

LC-MS/MS data analysis
Liquid chromatography with tandem mass spectrometry (LC-MS/MS) data were first processed by the multiplexed post experimental monoisotopic mass refinement (mPE-MMR) method, as previously described.
64
The refined data were searched against uniprot
Arabidopsis thaliana
reference database (released November 2015; 33,434 entries) and common contaminants (179 entries) using MS-GF + search engine (V9949).
65
Semi-tryptic cleavage allowance and precursor mass tolerance of 10 ppm were used for MS-GF + parameters. For global proteome analysis, TMT to lysine, and N-terminus and carbamidomethylation to cysteine, were used as static modifications. Oxidation to methionine and deamidation to asparagine and glutamine were used as variable modifications. For phosphoproteome analysis, the variable modifications of phosphorylation to serine, threonine, or tyrosine were added. The peptide spectrum matches (PSMs) were obtained using a false discovery rate (FDR) of 0.01. For phosphoproteome data, an additional search for unassigned spectra was performed after excluding PSMs from MS-GF + using MODplus search engine.
66
The variables, parameters, and databases of MODplus were the same as those of MS-GF+. The PSMs at FDR of 0.01 from MODplus were also used for analysis.
Protein and phosphosite inference
The peptides with 100% precursor isolation purity (PIP) detected in more than half of the experiments (≥2) were used for protein inference. The peptides were rolled up to infer the protein groups using bipartite graph analysis.
75
Representative proteins for each group were selected from those with the largest number of peptides. For the analysis of the global proteome, the protein groups peptide numbers ≥2, maximum protein coverage ≥25%, and unique coding-genes within groups were used. For phosphoproteome data, peptides were rolled up to infer the phosphosite groups, instead of protein groups. Thus, the representative phosphosites of protein for each group was selected. The phosphosite groups with peptide numbers ≥1 and unique coding-genes within groups were used for phosphoproteome analysis.

Identification of DEPeptides, DEPs, and DEPsites
The peptides having intensity values more than 50% of each comparison condition were used for identifying differentially expressed peptides (DEPeptides). The t-statistical values and log
2
-fold-changes were first obtained using Student’s t-test and median-ratio for each comparison. Empirical null distribution of t-statistical values was then estimated from random permutated intensity matrix (1,000 times). The adjusted
p
-values (Pt) were calculated by two-tailed tests for the observed t-statistical values using the empirical distributions. The peptides with Pt < 0.05 and an absolute value of log2-fold-changes >0.58 (1.5-fold-change) were selected as DEPeptides. The protein groups with DEPeptide numbers ≥2, except proteins having both up- and down-regulated DEPeptides, were identified as differentially expressed proteins (DEPs) in the global proteome. For the phosphoproteome, the phosphosite groups with DEPeptide numbers ≥2, except for phosphosites having both up- and down-regulated DEPeptides, were identified as differentially expressed phosphosites (DEPsites).
